terms.gloss: it escapes me, I don’t notice or remember
terms.grammar: phrase: fugiō with the accusative of the person; the thing as subject, or an indirect question
evidence: Cic. Rep. 2, 12: id quod fugit Lacedaemonium Lycūrgum (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Att. 7.18.3: dē Dionysiō, fugit mē ad tē anteā scrībere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The thing that escapes one is the subject: fugit mē ratiō (Catull. 10.29). Also nōn mē fugit, I am well aware.

terms.gloss: escape the notice of; go unnoticed
terms.comment: In this sense mostly impersonal in Cicero and Caesar: neque hoc tē fallit, you are well aware of this. Of a person, to go unnoticed (Liv. 22.33.1). Its everyday sense is to deceive.

phrases.latin: tantō silentiō in summum ēvāsēre ut nōn custōdēs sōlum fallerent, sed nē canēs quidem, sollicitum animal ad nocturnōs strepitūs, excitārent
phrases.english: they reached the top so quietly that they slipped past not only the guards but even the dogs, creatures alert to noises in the night, without waking them
